short: The SAND domain is a small DNA-binding fold named after the four proteins in which it was first recognized: Sp100, AIRE, NucP41/75 and DEAF1. Sequence-specific binding depends on a conserved KDWK motif on the domain's surface, and only some SAND proteins have it. The best-defined members are GMEB1 and GMEB2, which bind as a heterodimer, also known as parvovirus initiation factor, to two CpG-containing tetranucleotide half-sites with flexible spacing: ACGY-N(1-9)-RCGY, with an optimum spacer of six bases. Binding is abolished by methylation of the CpG in either half-site. AIRE and the speckled proteins SP100 and SP140 lack the KDWK motif and are recruited through chromatin rather than sequence, so motif models attributed to them should be treated as descriptions of where they were found.
long:
## The factors

SAND is a fold, not a functional group. The domain was named from Sp100, AIRE-1, NucP41/75 and
DEAF1, and its NMR structure showed a novel alpha-beta fold whose DNA-binding activity maps to a
conserved surface motif, KDWK, which gives the family its alternative name. Human SAND proteins
fall into distinct groups. GMEB1 and GMEB2 (p96 and p79) were identified twice over: as the
heterodimer that binds the glucocorticoid modulatory element upstream of the tyrosine
aminotransferase gene, and as parvovirus initiation factor, the host factor required for
minute virus of mice origin nicking. They carry the KDWK motif, bind DNA cooperatively, and are
ubiquitously expressed. DEAF1 (NUDR) is a related KDWK protein that binds TTCG-containing repeats;
notably, it has no motif in any of the four databases used here despite being named in this
family's definition. The speckled proteins SP100, SP110, SP140 and SP140L are nuclear-body
components that combine a SAND domain with PHD fingers and bromodomains and act as chromatin
readers in immune cells. AIRE, the autoimmune regulator, is the most important special case: its
SAND domain lacks the KDWK residues required for sequence-specific DNA contact and instead mediates
homodimerization, while its two PHD fingers read histone H3, PHD1 binding H3 tails that are
unmethylated at lysine 4. AIRE is essentially restricted to medullary thymic epithelial cells.

## The motif

For GMEB1/GMEB2 the site is well defined and unusual. Degenerate oligonucleotide selection showed
that the heterodimer, and each homodimer, binds two tetranucleotide half-sites conforming to
ACGY-N(1-9)-RCGY, with an optimum spacer of six bases; the spacing is genuinely flexible, so the
element is a pair of short half-sites at variable distance rather than a fixed-width motif. The
invariant feature is the CpG in each half-site, and 5-methylation of those cytosines abolishes
binding completely, which makes GMEB an unusual example of a factor whose occupancy is directly
methylation-sensitive at its core. Because CpG is suppressed in vertebrate genomes, such sites
should be rare, yet over half of a sample of 100 human promoters contained at least one, often
within 100 bases of the start site. The models in these databases capture only part of this
grammar. Most GMEB matrices collapse the pair into a single half-site region: the representative
model here is TACGTAA, and JASPAR's GMEB1 and GMEB2 matrices are tACGTa and TACGTAA. One CIS-BP
model, M05735_2.00, does show the doubled form (TACGTACGGTACGTA), which is the two half-sites
resolved. The consequence for scanning is severe: a six- or seven-base ACGT-centered model sits in
the middle of the sequence space used by bZIP factors, since TACGTA, TGACGT and CACGTG all contain
ACGT, and the data reflect this directly. Two GMEB1 models have a higher similarity to their
best out-of-family neighbour than to any in-family motif, and the family's cohesion is only 0.70
across 15 motifs. The remaining models are not ACGT elements at all: the ChIP-derived GMEB models
are GCGTCAGCGCG-like, the HOCOMOCO SP100 model is AACGGTTA and the SP140 model is GTCGTCACTA, each
with zero label agreement, and the Vierstra AIRE archetype (AC0160) is a CCAAT-containing element
rather than anything resembling a SAND site.

## Where it acts

GMEB sites are promoter-proximal and, by construction, CpG-containing, so they concentrate in
CpG-island promoters where their methylation sensitivity could make them responsive to DNA
methylation state. The glucocorticoid modulatory element itself modulates the sensitivity of a
glucocorticoid-responsive promoter rather than driving it, so GMEB acts as a modifier of another
factor's output. AIRE acts in a completely different regime: in medullary thymic epithelial cells
it associates with super-enhancers and with thousands of promoters of tissue-restricted antigen
genes, and its principal mechanism is releasing stalled RNA polymerase II rather than recruiting it
to a specific sequence. SP140 occupies and maintains repressed loci in macrophages, including
lineage-inappropriate developmental genes.

## Biology and disease

Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in AIRE cause autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal
dystrophy (APECED, also APS-1), a monogenic autoimmune disease; Aire-deficient mice lose promiscuous
expression of thousands of tissue-restricted antigens in the thymus and develop multi-organ
autoimmunity, which established the central-tolerance model of negative selection. Missense
mutations in the SAND domain of DEAF1 cause intellectual disability with severe speech impairment
and behavioral problems. Variants at SP140 and SP110 are associated with Crohn disease, multiple
sclerosis and chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and SP110 mutations cause hepatic venoocclusive disease
with immunodeficiency. GMEB proteins have no established monogenic disease link, but they are
required for parvovirus DNA replication.

## Reading a hit

The central caution is that this key mixes proteins that read sequence with proteins that do not. A
match to a GMEB model is a real, if weak, claim: look for the second CpG half-site within nine bases
and check the methylation state, because an unmethylated CpG is part of the site rather than
incidental. A match to an AIRE, SP100 or SP140 model is much harder to interpret. None of these
proteins has the KDWK motif required for sequence-specific SAND binding, their models here come from
integrative and ChIP-based evidence, their nearest neighbours lie in other families, and in AIRE's
case the archetype is a CCAAT-type element. The general risk for the ACGT-centered GMEB models is
confusion with bZIP sites, which share the same four-base core and are far more abundant; a TACGTA
match in a promoter is more likely to be a CRE-like or MAF-like element than a GMEB site.
caveats: Split this family in two before trusting anything. GMEB1 and GMEB2 have the KDWK motif and a real, if unusual, site: two CpG-containing half-sites with a 1-9 base spacer, abolished by CpG methylation. But the matrices compress this to a six- or seven-base ACGT core that overlaps bZIP space, and two GMEB1 models here match an out-of-family motif better than any relative. AIRE, SP100 and SP140 lack the KDWK residues needed for sequence-specific SAND binding; their models come from ChIP and integrative evidence, carry zero label agreement, and the Vierstra AIRE archetype is a CCAAT-type element. Treat those as records of where the protein was found. DEAF1 has no motif here at all.
